title: Measuring crowds: counts, trajectories and density
summary: Every model starts from measurements. Learn to get density, speed and flow from counts and trajectories, and why the Voronoi method gives smoother, fairer densities than counting heads in a box.
outcomes: compute density, speed and flow from trajectory data
explain classical and Voronoi density and when each is better
check that J = ρ × v holds in your own measurements
name the main open datasets and tools for crowd measurement
narration_en: Before you can model a crowd, you have to measure it. The richest data are trajectories: the position of every person, many times a second, extracted from video. Researchers at Forschungszentrum Jülich and partners have run hundreds of laboratory experiments and published the trajectories openly. From trajectories you can compute the three basic quantities. Density can be measured the classical way, by counting heads in a measurement area and dividing by its area, but that number jumps every time someone steps in or out. The Voronoi method gives each person the patch of floor closer to them than to anyone else; density inside the area is then the average of one over each patch's size, weighted by how much of the patch lies inside. It is smoother and responds to small changes. Speed comes from the change in position over time, and flow from counting people crossing a line. In this module you will compute all three from synthetic trajectories, and check that flow equals density times speed.
narration_ar: قبل أن تبني نموذجاً للحشد، عليك أن تقيسه. وأغنى البيانات هي المسارات: موضع كل شخص مرات كثيرة في الثانية، مستخرجاً من الفيديو. وقد أجرى باحثون في مركز يوليش للأبحاث وشركاؤهم مئات التجارب المخبرية ونشروا المسارات علناً. ومن المسارات تستطيع أن تحسب الكميات الأساسية الثلاث. يمكن قياس الكثافة بالطريقة التقليدية، بعدّ الرؤوس في منطقة قياس وقسمتها على مساحتها، لكن هذا الرقم يقفز كلما دخل شخص أو خرج. أما طريقة فورونوي فتعطي كل شخص رقعة الأرض الأقرب إليه منها إلى أي شخص آخر؛ ثم تكون الكثافة داخل المنطقة متوسط مقلوب مساحة كل رقعة، موزوناً بالجزء الواقع منها داخل المنطقة. وهي أنعم وتستجيب للتغيرات الصغيرة. وتأتي السرعة من تغيّر الموضع عبر الزمن، ويأتي التدفق من عدّ الأشخاص الذين يعبرون خطاً. ستحسب في هذه الوحدة الكميات الثلاث من مسارات مصطنعة، وتتحقق من أن التدفق يساوي الكثافة مضروبة في السرعة.

diagram.title: From video to the fundamental diagram
diagram.caption: Trajectories feed three measurements; together they give the fundamental diagram that every model must reproduce.

nodes.label: Video
nodes.detail: Overhead cameras record the scene. Software such as PeTrack (Jülich) detects heads and tracks them frame by frame.

nodes.label: Trajectories
nodes.sub: x, y, t for each person
nodes.detail: Positions of each person over time, usually at 16 to 25 frames per second, corrected for camera distortion.

nodes.label: Density
nodes.detail: Classical: count in the area ÷ area. Voronoi: average of 1 ÷ cell area over the measurement area (Steffen and Seyfried 2010).

nodes.label: Speed
nodes.detail: Each person's speed from positions a short time apart; the area speed averages over the people (or Voronoi cells) inside.

nodes.label: Flow
nodes.detail: Count people crossing a line per second; divide by width for specific flow.

nodes.label: Fundamental diagram
nodes.detail: Plot speed or flow against density for many time windows. Check J ≈ ρ × v. Compare with other studies and models.

sections.heading: Trajectories
sections.html: The richest crowd data are trajectories: (x, y) positions of each person at each time. They come from overhead video processed by tracking software such as PeTrack, or from experiments where participants wear coloured caps. The Jülich pedestrian dynamics data archive publishes hundreds of such experiments.

sections.heading: Classical and Voronoi density
sections.html:
Classical density counts people in a measurement area A: ρ = N ÷ A. It jumps by 1 ÷ A each time someone enters or leaves. Voronoi density (Steffen and Seyfried 2010) gives each person i the region closer to them than to anyone else (area Ai) and averages:

ρV = (1 ÷ A) × Σi (area of cell i inside the box) ÷ Ai

It varies smoothly, works in small areas, and reduces scatter in fundamental diagrams.

sections.heading: Speed and flow
sections.html: Speed is distance moved over a short time: v = Δx ÷ Δt, usually over 0.5 to 1 s to smooth out the sway of each step. Flow is the number of people crossing a line in a time window, divided by the window, and by the width for specific flow. In a steady crowd, the three must agree: J ≈ ρ × v. If they do not, check the measurement area, time window or tracking.

sections.heading: Beyond the laboratory
sections.html: Real events rarely have overhead cameras everywhere. Practitioners combine counts (gates, turnstiles, ticket scans), CCTV with computer-vision counting (module 3.4), and phone-based data such as Wi-Fi probes or network data. Each has errors and privacy issues: report both.

callouts.title: See it
callouts.html: In the explorer, move the seed slider: the classical density in the box jumps between snapshots, while the Voronoi density changes more smoothly.

callouts.title: Edge effects
callouts.html: Voronoi cells at the edge of the crowd are unbounded. Cut them at a sensible distance or with walls, as PedPy does.

code.title: Density, speed and flow from trajectories
code.explain: Synthetic one-way corridor. Computes classical density, mean speed, flow across a line and a Voronoi-style density for one frame. Replace the synthetic trajectories with data from the Jülich archive.
code.expected:
people crossing x = 12 m: 120 in 60 s -> flow 2.00 per s, 0.50 per m per s
mean classical density 0.42 per m2 (all frames), mean speed 1.14 m/s
check J = rho * v: 0.50 per m per s
frame 300: classical 1.00 per m2, Voronoi 0.96 per m2

takeaways: Trajectories give density, speed and flow; the Jülich archive and PedPy make them accessible.
Classical density jumps; Voronoi density is smoother and works in small areas.
J ≈ ρ × v is a built-in check on your measurements.
Field data combine counts, CCTV and phone data, each with errors and privacy issues.

quiz.q: Classical density in a 16 m² area with 24 people is…
A Voronoi cell of a person is…
options: The region closer to them than to anyone else
quiz.explain: Each point of floor belongs to its nearest person.

quiz.q: Why measure speed over about a second?
options: To smooth out the sideways sway of each step
quiz.explain: Step sway adds noise at short intervals.

quiz.q: Your measured flow is much larger than density × speed. What should you suspect?
options: A measurement error: area, time window or tracking
quiz.explain: In steady flow they should agree.
